title: A New King and a Growing People
summary: The seventy descendants of Jacob multiply in Egypt until the land is filled with them. A new king who does not know Joseph fears their numbers, forces them into brutal labor building store cities, and when they keep multiplying, orders the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys. The midwives fear God and let the boys live, so Pharaoh commands all his people to throw every Hebrew son into the Nile.
story: Exodus begins by repeating the names of Jacob's sons who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46), tying the two books together. Then the generation of Joseph dies, and time passes. What Genesis promised is coming true: God told Abraham his descendants would be as many as the stars (15:5), and here they are fruitful, increase, and fill the land, in words that echo God's blessing on humanity at creation (Genesis 1:28). But God also told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own, enslaved and mistreated (15:13). This chapter shows both halves of that word arriving at once. It sets the stage for everything that follows: a people who belong to God, held by a king who claims them for himself, and a threat to their children that the birth of Moses in Exodus 2 will answer.
historical:
The chapter never names the king. Those who date the exodus around 1446 BC look to the powerful Pharaohs of the Eighteenth Dynasty, while those who prefer the thirteenth century BC think of Seti I or his son Ramesses II. Either way, the new king who did not know Joseph belongs to a dynasty that no longer honored the memory of a Semitic official or his people. Some scholars connect his fear of foreigners in the eastern Delta joining an enemy (v. 10) with Egypt's expulsion of the Hyksos, Semitic rulers of the Delta, around 1550 BC.

The store cities Pithom and Rameses (v. 11) were in the eastern Delta. Rameses is usually identified with Pi-Ramesse, the great residence of Ramesses II near modern Qantir, which is one reason many scholars favor a thirteenth-century date; others think the name is a later updating, as in Genesis 47:11. Pithom, meaning house of the god Atum, is placed by most scholars in the Wadi Tumilat, though whether at Tell el-Maskhuta or Tell er-Retabeh is debated. Egyptian building relied on sun-dried mud brick, and a painting in the tomb of Rekhmire, a vizier in the fifteenth century BC, shows laborers, some of them foreigners, making bricks under overseers.
cultural:
Egypt's economy depended on large labor forces, drawn from peasants during the flood season and from prisoners of war and foreigners. The Hebrew for forced labor (mas) is the term later used for the conscripted labor of Solomon's building projects (1 Kings 5:13), a detail Israel's historians did not hide.

Egyptian women commonly gave birth kneeling or squatting on a pair of bricks or stones, which is probably what the birthstools of verse 16 refer to; a painted birth brick from the Middle Kingdom has been found at Abydos. Midwives were trusted women of the community. It is not certain whether Shiphrah and Puah were Hebrews or Egyptian women who served the Hebrews, since the Hebrew can be read either way. Later Jewish tradition identified them with Moses' mother and sister. The Nile was the source of all Egypt's life, and its annual flood was personified as a god. Pharaoh's order to throw the boys into it turns the river of life into an instrument of death.
literary: The chapter is built as a sequence of three escalating attempts by Pharaoh to control Israel, each of which fails: forced labor (vv. 8-14), secret murder by the midwives (vv. 15-21), and open murder by the whole nation (v. 22). Verse 7 piles up five verbs of increase (fruitful, increased, multiplied, exceedingly numerous, filled), language drawn from Genesis 1 and 9, so that Pharaoh's policy is set against God's creation blessing. His words “Come, let us deal shrewdly” echo the builders of Babel, who also said come, let us (Genesis 11:3-4). Verses 13 and 14 repeat the root for serve or work five times in Hebrew, pressing home the weight of the slavery. There is irony throughout: the king fears the Hebrews will leave the country, which is exactly what will happen, and the Nile he uses to destroy them will be the river from which their deliverer is drawn. The narrator also makes a quiet point of values: the king of Egypt is never named, but two midwives are.

outline.t: Jacob's family grows into a people
A new king and the bitterness of forced labor
The midwives fear God and let the boys live
Pharaoh orders every Hebrew son thrown into the Nile

doctrines.note: “The more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished” (v. 12). The chapter shows God keeping his promise of a great nation even under a hostile empire. Pharaoh's power is real, but it cannot stop what God has said he will do, and every measure he takes to shrink Israel fails.

The chapter does not soften Israel's suffering. Their lives are made bitter, their labor is ruthless, and their sons are marked for death. God is barely mentioned until the midwives appear; the first readers learn that God's silence is not the same as his absence, and that his people's suffering is seen.

The midwives feared God and did not do as the king commanded (v. 17). Fear of God in the Old Testament is reverent trust that takes God more seriously than any human power. For two women with no status, it meant defying the most powerful man in the world, and God honored them with families of their own.

words.note: Avad, to work or serve. In verses 13 and 14 the Egyptians make the Israelites serve with rigor, and the root recurs five times. The same verb is used for serving God in worship, and Exodus turns on that double meaning: Israel will be freed from serving Pharaoh so that they may serve the LORD (for example 4:23; 8:1).

Yare, to fear, and in relation to God, to revere. The midwives feared God (vv. 17, 21), and so did not fear Pharaoh. The Old Testament presents the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10), a response to God's greatness that frees a person from lesser fears.

Ivri, Hebrew. In the Old Testament the word is used mainly by foreigners speaking about Israelites or by Israelites identifying themselves to foreigners, as here in the mouth of the king of Egypt. Some scholars connect it with the habiru or apiru, a term in second-millennium texts for displaced people on the margins of society, but the relationship is debated.

christ: Matthew tells the story of Jesus' birth in a way that recalls this chapter. As Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew boys killed, King Herod ordered the killing of the boys of Bethlehem, and the child Jesus escaped, as Moses would, from a murderous king (Matthew 2:13-18). Matthew does not quote Exodus 1, but many readers see him presenting Jesus as the one who relives Israel's story and brings it to its goal: the child whose life was threatened by a tyrant becomes the deliverer. The midwives' choice to obey God rather than the king anticipates the apostles' words to the council that they must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The link to Christ here is a pattern rather than a prediction. The chapter shows the kind of darkness into which God sends deliverers, and the Gospels show him doing it again, finally, in Jesus.

hard.q: Did the midwives lie to Pharaoh, and did God reward them for it?
hard.a:
The midwives told Pharaoh that Hebrew women gave birth before a midwife could arrive (v. 19). The text does not say whether this was true, partly true, or a cover story, though most readers take it as a deception meant to protect the babies. What the text does say is why God blessed them: “because the midwives feared God” (v. 21). The reward is tied to their fear of God and their refusal to kill, not explicitly to their words.

Christians have weighed the case differently. Augustine held that lying is always wrong and argued that God rewarded the midwives' mercy, not their falsehood. Many others, pointing to Rahab (Joshua 2; Hebrews 11:31) and to people who have hidden the innocent from murderous regimes, argue that deceiving someone who is seeking to kill the innocent is not the false witness the commandment forbids, since the would-be killer has no right to the truth he would use for murder. Both views agree that the midwives did right to refuse Pharaoh's order, and that their courage is held up for honor.

questions: The midwives feared God more than Pharaoh. What pressures in your life compete with the fear of God, and what would it look like to take God more seriously than them?

Pharaoh's cruelty begins with fear: “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us.” How does fear of a group of people turn into policies of cruelty, and where do you see that pattern today?
The narrator names two midwives but never names the king of Egypt. What does that suggest about whose lives matter most in God's story?
